chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting ready and talking with your provider

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding health information you can trust
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tell a trustworthy health source from an untrustworthy one.
This lesson builds toward: Given a health website or post, you will check whether the source is trustworthy and look up a health word on a trusted site such as medlineplus.gov, writing the meaning in your own words.
Health information is everywhere: websites, social media, TV ads, friends and AI chatbots. Some of it is excellent. Some is old, wrong or trying to sell you something.
Good free places to start in the US: MedlinePlus (medlineplus.gov) from the National Library of Medicine, the CDC (cdc.gov), and the National Institutes of Health (nih.gov). Official US government sites end in .gov. Hospitals, universities and well-known medical groups are often good too.
Ask four questions about any source: Who wrote it? When was it updated? Is it trying to sell me something? Does it match what other trusted sources say? An AI assistant can explain a hard medical word in simple language, but it can be wrong. Check what it says on a trusted site, and never type your full name, ID or insurance numbers into it. Your doctor or pharmacist has the final word for you.
Step by step:
- Find who made the page.
- Look for the date it was updated.
- Check if it is selling something.
- Compare with MedlinePlus or another .gov site.
- Bring your questions to your doctor or pharmacist.
Words to know:
- Health literacy: being able to find, understand and use health information to make decisions.
- MedlinePlus: a free US government health information website from the National Library of Medicine.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Health Literacy
- CDC: What Is Health Literacy?
Try it now: Pick a health word you have heard but do not fully understand (for example blood pressure, cholesterol or asthma). Look it up on medlineplus.gov and write a one-sentence meaning in your own words.
You can now find health information on trusted sites and check any source with four simple questions.

check.q: Which detail makes a health website more trustworthy?
options: It sells a product on every page
It has lots of exclamation marks
It shows who wrote it and when it was last updated
It promises a cure
check.why: Knowing who wrote it and when helps you judge the information.

check.q: A friend shares a post saying a tea cures high blood pressure. What would you do?
options: Stop your blood pressure medicine
Share it with family
Buy the tea right away
Check a trusted site and ask your doctor
check.why: Health claims are checked on trusted sites and with your provider.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Preparing for a medical visit
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a visit sheet with your concern, questions and medicine list.
This lesson builds toward: Before a medical visit, you will write a visit sheet with your concern, your top three questions and a full medicine list, with when the symptom started and what makes it better or worse.
Visits are often short. Preparing ahead helps you remember everything and helps the provider understand you. MedlinePlus suggests writing down your questions, describing your symptoms in writing, and listing your allergies and every medicine, herb, vitamin and supplement you take.
For a symptom, write: what it is, when it started, how often it happens, what makes it better or worse, and what you have tried. Put your top three questions first, so the most important ones get answered.
You can bring a trusted friend or family member to listen and take notes. If you need an interpreter, ask the office ahead of time to arrange one. Bring your insurance or Medicare card, a photo ID and your medicine list or the bottles themselves.
Step by step:
- Write your concern: what, when it started, how often, what helps or hurts.
- Write your top three questions.
- List every medicine, vitamin, supplement and allergy.
- Ask someone to come with you if it helps.
- Ask for an interpreter ahead of time if you need one.
Words to know:
- Provider: a doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or other professional who gives health care.
- Symptom: a change in your body or mind that you notice, like pain, a cough or tiredness.
- Supplement: a vitamin, mineral, herb or other product you take to add to your diet.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Talking With Your Doctor
Try it now: Start your visit sheet. Write one real or practice concern with when it started and what makes it better or worse, then your top three questions.
You can now prepare a visit sheet with your concern, your top questions and what to bring.

check.q: Why bring a full medicine list to a visit?
options: So the doctor can check everything you take works safely together
Because it is required to get in
So you do not need to talk
To show you take a lot
check.why: A full list helps your provider avoid harmful mixes and mistakes.

check.q: You have five worries but a short appointment. What would you do?
options: Bring none of them up
Write your top three questions and ask the most important first
Talk very fast about all five
Save them all for next year
check.why: Putting your top questions first makes sure the most important ones are answered.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: During the visit: asking questions and checking you understood
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask questions until you understand and repeat the plan back in your own words.
This lesson builds toward: During a visit or role-play, you will ask questions until you understand and repeat the plan back in your own words, covering what the problem is, what to do and why.
You have the right to understand your care. If the provider uses a word you do not know, say: "Can you explain that in simpler words?" If they go too fast, say: "Can you slow down?" You can ask them to write instructions down.
Three questions cover most visits: What is my main problem? What do I need to do? Why is it important for me to do this? Keep asking until you can answer all three.
Before you leave, use teach-back: say the plan back in your own words. "So I take one pill each morning with food, and I come back in two weeks. If my ankle swells, I call you." If you missed something, the provider can fix it right then. Also ask how to reach the office later and what to do if things get worse.
Step by step:
- Ask what any unknown word means.
- Ask the three questions: main problem, what to do, why.
- Take notes or have your helper take them.
- Say the plan back in your own words (teach-back).
- Ask how to reach the office and what to do if things get worse.
Words to know:
- Teach-back: saying the plan back in your own words to check you understood it.
- Follow-up: a later visit or call to check how you are doing.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Talking With Your Doctor
Try it now: Role-play with a friend or say it out loud: your friend reads a short doctor's instruction (for example "Take this twice a day for 10 days and finish it all"). Ask one question about it, then teach it back in your own words.
You can now ask clear questions during a visit and use teach-back to check you understood the plan.

check.q: Which is one of the three key questions to ask at a visit?
options: How much does the doctor earn?
Why is it important for me to do this?
Can I skip my medicine?
How long is the wait?
check.why: The three key questions are: what is my main problem, what do I need to do, and why is it important.

check.q: The doctor says to take a pill "twice daily with food." What would you do before leaving?
options: Nod and leave
Ask a stranger in the waiting room
Say it back: "So I take it at breakfast and dinner with food, right?"
Guess later at home
check.why: Teach-back checks that you understood the plan correctly.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Medicines: reading the label and keeping a list
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read a medicine label and keep an up-to-date medicine list.
This lesson builds toward: Given a medicine, vitamin or supplement, you will read the label and add it to your medicine list with name, dose, how often, what it is for and a warning, with one question written for a pharmacist.
Medicine mistakes are common and often preventable. MedlinePlus advises keeping a list of every medicine with its dose and when you take it, including over-the-counter products, vitamins, supplements and herbs, plus any allergies, and bringing it to every visit.
Read the label every time, not from memory. Look for: the medicine name, how much to take (the dose), how often and when, how long, warnings (for example "may cause drowsiness" or "take with food"), and the refill and expiration information. Over-the-counter medicines have a Drug Facts label with uses, warnings and directions.
Your pharmacist is a free expert. Ask: Why am I taking this? What side effects are common and what should I do? When should I stop? Is it safe with my other medicines and supplements? Do I need to avoid any foods or alcohol? Never stop or change a prescribed medicine without asking your doctor or pharmacist first.
Step by step:
- Read the name, dose, how often and how long.
- Read the warnings.
- Add it to your medicine list with the dose and time.
- Ask the pharmacist your questions.
- Bring the list to every visit and update it when anything changes.
Words to know:
- Dose: how much of a medicine to take at one time.
- Over-the-counter (OTC): medicine you can buy without a prescription.
- Side effect: an extra effect of a medicine that you did not want, like an upset stomach.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Medication Errors
Try it now: Take one medicine, vitamin or supplement you (or a family member) use. Read the label and add it to your medicine list: name, dose, how often, what it is for and one warning. Write one question to ask a pharmacist.
You can now read a medicine label, keep a complete medicine list and ask a pharmacist the right questions.

check.q: What does "dose" mean on a medicine label?
options: How much medicine to take at one time
The price of the medicine
The date it was made
The name of the pharmacy
check.why: The dose is the amount you take at one time.

check.q: You start a new vitamin. What would you do with your medicine list?
options: Leave it off because vitamins do not count
Wait until your next birthday
Only tell your friends
Add it to the list and ask the pharmacist if it is safe with your other medicines
check.why: Vitamins and supplements belong on the list and can mix with medicines.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Test results, patient portals and your records
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a test result in a patient portal and write questions about it.
This lesson builds toward: Using a patient portal or your clinic, you will find a test result or visit note and write questions about it, with at least two questions for your provider.
Many clinics and hospitals have a patient portal: a secure website or app where you can see test results, visit notes and upcoming appointments, request refills, and message your care team. MedlinePlus recommends learning how to access your records so you can keep track of results, treatment plans and medicines. Veterans can use VA's online tools; ask your VA team how to sign up.
Test results often show your number next to a "normal" or reference range. A result marked high or low is not always a problem; it depends on you, your history and other results. Do not panic and do not change your treatment on your own. Write down questions and ask your provider what the result means for you.
Keep your portal safe: use a strong password, never share it, and sign out on shared or library computers. If you need help signing up, call the clinic's front desk. A family member or caregiver can often get access with your permission; ask the office how.
Step by step:
- Ask your clinic how to sign up for the patient portal.
- Find your latest test result.
- Look at your number and the reference range.
- Write questions: What does this mean for me? Do I need to do anything?
- Send the question through the portal or ask at your next visit.
Words to know:
- Patient portal: a secure website or app where you see your health records and message your care team.
- Reference range: the range of results that is usual for most healthy people.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Talking With Your Doctor
Try it now: If you have a patient portal, sign in and find one recent result or visit note. If you don't, call or ask your clinic how to sign up. Either way, write two questions you would ask about a test result.
You can now use a patient portal safely, read a result next to its reference range and ask your provider what it means for you.

check.q: What can you usually do in a patient portal?
options: Change your own prescriptions
See your records and message your care team
Order medicine without a prescription
Read other patients' results
check.why: A portal is a secure place to see your records and message your care team.

check.q: You used a library computer to check your portal. What would you do when you finish?
options: Leave it open for next time
Write your password on a note by the computer
Sign out and close the browser
Turn off the screen only
check.why: Signing out on shared computers keeps your health records private.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Health coverage words and your visit kit
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain common health coverage words and know who to ask about costs.
This lesson builds toward: Given common health coverage words, you will explain words such as deductible, copay and in-network and name who to ask about costs, in your own words without help.
Cost words confuse almost everyone. HealthCare.gov defines them. A premium is what you pay for your plan, usually each month. A deductible is the amount you pay for covered care before your plan starts to pay. A copayment (copay) is a set dollar amount you pay for a covered service, such as a visit. In-network providers have a contract with your plan and usually cost you less.
Before a test or visit, you can ask: "Is this provider in my network?" "About how much will I pay?" Call the number on your insurance card. Medicare: call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week except some federal holidays. Veterans can ask the VA about their benefits. Many community health centers offer care on a sliding scale based on income; search findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov and ask the center about fees.
Now put it together. Your visit kit is your visit sheet (concern and top questions), your medicine list, your insurance card and ID, and a pen or phone for notes. After the visit, write the plan in your own words.
Step by step:
- Learn four words: premium, deductible, copay, in-network.
- Before care, ask if the provider is in your network and what you may pay.
- Call the number on your card, or 1-800-MEDICARE for Medicare.
- Pack your visit kit: visit sheet, medicine list, card, ID, notes.
- After the visit, write the plan in your own words.
Words to know:
- Premium: what you pay for your health plan, usually every month.
- Deductible: what you pay for covered care before your plan starts to pay.
- Copay: a set dollar amount you pay for a covered service.
- In-network: providers that have a contract with your plan; they usually cost you less.
Official sources:
- HealthCare.gov Glossary: Deductible
- HealthCare.gov Glossary: Copayment
- Medicare.gov: Talk to Someone
- HRSA: Find a Health Center
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page visit sheet with your concern, your top three questions and your full medicine list. After a real visit, or a practice run with a friend playing the doctor, write the plan in your own words: the main problem, what to do, and why.
You can now explain common coverage words, ask about costs before care, and bring a complete visit kit to every appointment.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Symptom note The concern is vague, or it is missing when it started. Says what the concern is, when it started and what makes it better or worse. Also notes how it affects daily life. Top three questions Fewer than three questions, or they are unclear. Three clear questions with the most important first. Includes the three key questions: the problem, what to do and why. Medicine list Missing over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, supplements or allergies. Every prescription, over-the-counter medicine, vitamin, supplement and allergy, with dose and how often. Also lists what each one is for and a question for the pharmacist. Plan in your own words The plan is missing, or copies the doctor's words without understanding. Says the main problem, what to do and why, in the learner's own words. Also notes how to reach the office and what to do if things get worse. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: The provider is on social media
The provider is in your neighborhood
The provider is free
The provider has a contract with your plan and usually costs you less
check.why: In-network providers have a contract with your plan.

check.q: You are unsure what a visit will cost you. What would you do?
options: Ask your plan or the office about costs before the visit
Skip the visit
Guess and hope
Ask a stranger online
check.why: Your plan or the office can tell you about costs ahead of time.
